### Slot Card (`custom:lcm-slot`)

Primary card for managing individual code slots. Features:

- **Inline editing**: Name and PIN editable directly in card
- **Condition management**: Add/edit/remove condition entity via dialog
- **Lock status**: Per-lock sync status, actual code on lock (masked/revealed)
- **Collapsible sections**: Conditions and lock status can be collapsed
- **Real-time updates**: WebSocket subscription for instant state changes

**Config options:**

| Option | Default | Description |
| ------ | ------- | ----------- |
| `slot` | required | Slot number to display |
| `config_entry_id` | - | Config entry ID (or use `config_entry_title`) |
| `code_display` | `masked_with_reveal` | `masked`, `unmasked`, or `masked_with_reveal` |
| `show_conditions` | true | Show conditions section |
| `show_lock_status` | true | Show lock status section |
| `show_lock_sync` | true | Show sync status per lock |
| `show_code_sensors` | true | Show actual codes on locks |
| `show_lock_count` | true | Show lock count badge |
| `collapsed_sections` | [] | Sections to collapse by default: `conditions`, `lock_status` |

### Lock Codes Card (`custom:lcm-lock-codes`)

Lock-centric view showing all slots on a single lock (managed and unmanaged).

**Config options:**

| Option | Default | Description |
| ------ | ------- | ----------- |
| `lock_entity_id` | required | Lock entity to display slots for |
| `code_display` | `masked_with_reveal` | `masked`, `unmasked`, or `masked_with_reveal` |
| `title` | - | Optional card title override |

### Lovelace Strategies

- `custom:lock-code-manager` - Dashboard strategy auto-generating views per config entry
- `custom:lock-code-manager` - View strategy for a single config entry
- `custom:lock-code-manager-slot` - Section strategy for individual slots
- `custom:lock-code-manager-lock` - Section strategy for lock codes sections

### Condition Entities

Slots can have condition entities that control when the PIN is active. The PIN is only active when
the condition entity state is `on` (for calendars, this means an event is in progress).

**Supported domains** (defined in `CONDITION_ENTITY_DOMAINS` in `const.py`):

| Domain | Active When | Use Case |
| ------ | ----------- | -------- |
| `calendar` | Event in progress | Time-based access via calendar events |
| `schedule` | Within scheduled time range | HA Schedule helper for recurring windows |
| `binary_sensor` | State is `on` | Custom logic via templates, presence, etc. |
| `switch` | State is `on` | Manual toggle control |
| `input_boolean` | State is `on` | Simple on/off control via UI |

**UI Features:**

- Calendar and schedule entities show next event details in the slot card
- Condition can be added/edited/removed via the slot card's condition dialog

**Excluded Integrations:**

Some integrations create entities in supported domains but have state semantics incompatible with
access control. These are blocked via `EXCLUDED_CONDITION_PLATFORMS` in `const.py`:

| Integration | Reason |
| ----------- | ------ |
| `scheduler` (scheduler-component) | `on` means "schedule enabled", not "access allowed now" |

Validation occurs in both `config_flow.py` (UI configuration) and `websocket.py` (slot card editing).

Lock Code Manager is a Home Assistant custom integration that allows users to manage lock
usercodes across multiple locks. It reduces entity/automation sprawl compared to
alternatives by handling logic internally rather than generating numerous Home Assistant
entities.

- `git` and `gh` commands are automatically approved
- When making changes to ts files, before handing it back over to me, run yarn test and build and fix any issues.
- When making changes to python files, before handing it back over to me, run pytest in the venv and fix any issues.
- When creating a PR, ALWAYS use the .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md template
- When submitting a PR, note that Copilot will eventually add review comments which you must review -
  either make changes as needed or explain why you are not addressing a comment (comments that you make
  code changes for don't need a response). Resolve all comments as you address them or respond to them.
  Provide a summary of what was done or not done and ask for confirmation before committing the changes.
- When running hass or any other python driven commands, always run from the venv
- Before committing, ensure pre-commit checks succeed and tests pass.
- Use `prek` instead of `pre-commit` for running pre-commit checks (`prek run --all-files`).
  `prek` is a faster drop-in replacement.

- **Never amend commits after a PR has been created.** Always commit forward. Squash-on-merge
  handles the final cleanup. Separate commits show what changed in response to each review round.
- Force-push is only acceptable for rebasing onto an updated base branch, not for rewriting history.
- Tests go with code changes in the same PR. Test-only PRs are only for refactoring existing tests.

| `lock_code_manager/clear_unmanaged_code` | Clear a code on a slot LCM does not manage |
| `lock_code_manager/set_condition` | Add or edit a slot's condition entity |
| `lock_code_manager/clear_condition` | Remove a slot's condition entity |

## Frontend

### Slot Card (`custom:lcm-slot`)

Primary card for managing individual code slots. Features:

- **Inline editing**: Name and PIN editable directly in card
- **Condition management**: Add/edit/remove condition entity via dialog
- **Lock status**: Per-lock sync status, actual code on lock (masked/revealed)
- **Collapsible sections**: Conditions and lock status can be collapsed
- **Real-time updates**: WebSocket subscription for instant state changes

**Config options:**

| Option | Default | Description |
| ------ | ------- | ----------- |
| `slot` | required | Slot number to display |
| `config_entry_id` | - | Config entry ID (or use `config_entry_title`) |
| `code_display` | `masked_with_reveal` | `masked`, `unmasked`, or `masked_with_reveal` |
| `show_conditions` | true | Show conditions section |
| `show_lock_status` | true | Show lock status section |
| `show_lock_sync` | true | Show sync status per lock |
| `show_code_sensors` | true | Show actual codes on locks |
| `show_lock_count` | true | Show lock count badge |
| `collapsed_sections` | [] | Sections to collapse by default: `conditions`, `lock_status` |

### Lock Codes Card (`custom:lcm-lock-codes`)

Lock-centric view showing all slots on a single lock (managed and unmanaged).

**Config options:**

| Option | Default | Description |
| ------ | ------- | ----------- |
| `lock_entity_id` | required | Lock entity to display slots for |
| `code_display` | `masked_with_reveal` | `masked`, `unmasked`, or `masked_with_reveal` |
| `title` | - | Optional card title override |

### Lovelace Strategies

- `custom:lock-code-manager` - Dashboard strategy auto-generating views per config entry
- `custom:lock-code-manager` - View strategy for a single config entry
- `custom:lock-code-manager-slot` - Section strategy for individual slots
- `custom:lock-code-manager-lock` - Section strategy for lock codes sections

### Condition Entities

Slots can have condition entities that control when the PIN is active. The PIN is only active when
the condition entity state is `on` (for calendars, this means an event is in progress).

**Supported domains** (defined in `CONDITION_ENTITY_DOMAINS` in `const.py`):

| Domain | Active When | Use Case |
| ------ | ----------- | -------- |
| `calendar` | Event in progress | Time-based access via calendar events |
| `schedule` | Within scheduled time range | HA Schedule helper for recurring windows |
| `binary_sensor` | State is `on` | Custom logic via templates, presence, etc. |
| `switch` | State is `on` | Manual toggle control |
| `input_boolean` | State is `on` | Simple on/off control via UI |

**UI Features:**

- Calendar and schedule entities show next event details in the slot card
- Condition can be added/edited/removed via the slot card's condition dialog

**Excluded Integrations:**

Some integrations create entities in supported domains but have state semantics incompatible with
access control. These are blocked via `EXCLUDED_CONDITION_PLATFORMS` in `const.py`:

| Integration | Reason |
| ----------- | ------ |
| `scheduler` (scheduler-component) | `on` means "schedule enabled", not "access allowed now" |

Validation occurs in both `config_flow.py` (UI configuration) and `websocket.py` (slot card editing).

"""
A credential use is written to the logbook of what it was used against.

Home Assistant's logbook shows an entity only its own integration's described
events, and Lock Code Manager owns none of the locks it manages. So the entry
has to be a manual logbook entry, the one kind of event the logbook shows for
any entity whose ``entity_id`` it names. These tests query the logbook the way
a lock's more-info dialog does -- by the lock's entity ID -- so they fail if
the entry lands anywhere a person looking at the lock would not see it.
"""

from datetime import timedelta
import itertools
from typing import Any

import pytest
from pytest_homeassistant_custom_component.components.recorder.common import (
    async_wait_recording_done,
)

from homeassistant.components.logbook import DOMAIN as LOGBOOK_DOMAIN
from homeassistant.core import HomeAssistant
from homeassistant.setup import async_setup_component
from homeassistant.util import dt as dt_util

from custom_components.lock_code_manager.const import (
    ATTR_CODE,
    ATTR_SOURCE,
    ATTR_TARGET,
    DOMAIN,
    SERVICE_USE_CREDENTIAL,
)
from custom_components.lock_code_manager.model.credentials import CredentialType
from custom_components.lock_code_manager.model.events import (
    CredentialOperation,
    credential_use_message,
)
from custom_components.lock_code_manager.providers import BaseLock

from .common import LOCK_1_ENTITY_ID, LOCK_2_ENTITY_ID

EXTERNAL_KEYPAD = "sensor.side_gate_keypad"
EXTERNAL_TARGET = "cover.side_gate"


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def auto_enable_custom_integrations(recorder_db_url, enable_custom_integrations):
    """
    Claim the recorder database before Home Assistant starts.

    Overrides the project-wide autouse fixture of the same name, which pulls
    in `hass` before `recorder_db_url` may run.
    """
    yield


@pytest.fixture(name="logbook")
async def logbook_fixture(recorder_mock, hass: HomeAssistant) -> None:
    """Run the real logbook over the real recorder."""
    assert await async_setup_component(hass, LOGBOOK_DOMAIN, {})
    await hass.async_block_till_done()


async def _logbook_for(hass_ws_client, hass: HomeAssistant, entity_id: str) -> list:
    """Return the logbook entries for one entity, as its more-info dialog asks."""
    await async_wait_recording_done(hass)
    client = await hass_ws_client(hass)
    await client.send_json_auto_id(
        {
            "type": "logbook/get_events",
            "start_time": (dt_util.utcnow() - timedelta(hours=1)).isoformat(),
            "entity_ids": [entity_id],
        }
    )
    response = await client.receive_json()
    assert response["success"], response
    return response["result"]


def _uses(entries: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    """Keep the entries Lock Code Manager wrote, dropping the lock's own states."""
    return [entry for entry in entries if entry.get("domain") == DOMAIN]


async def test_a_lock_observed_use_is_in_the_locks_logbook(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    hass_ws_client,
    logbook,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
):
    """One use the lock observed is one entry on that lock, naming the user."""
    lock: BaseLock = lock_code_manager_config_entry.runtime_data.locks[LOCK_1_ENTITY_ID]
    lock.async_fire_code_slot_event(2, False, credential_type=CredentialType.PIN)
    await hass.async_block_till_done()

    uses = _uses(await _logbook_for(hass_ws_client, hass, LOCK_1_ENTITY_ID))
    assert len(uses) == 1
    assert uses[0]["entity_id"] == LOCK_1_ENTITY_ID
    assert uses[0]["name"] == "test2"
    assert uses[0]["message"] == "used a PIN to unlock"

    assert _uses(await _logbook_for(hass_ws_client, hass, LOCK_2_ENTITY_ID)) == []


async def test_a_reported_use_is_in_its_targets_logbook(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    hass_ws_client,
    logbook,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
):
    """
    A use reported through the action lands on its target, whatever that is.

    The target here is a cover no integration even provides: the entry names
    it, so the logbook files it there.
    """
    await hass.services.async_call(
        DOMAIN,
        SERVICE_USE_CREDENTIAL,
        {
            "config_entry_id": lock_code_manager_config_entry.entry_id,
            ATTR_CODE: "1234",
            ATTR_SOURCE: EXTERNAL_KEYPAD,
            ATTR_TARGET: EXTERNAL_TARGET,
        },
        blocking=True,
    )
    await hass.async_block_till_done()

    uses = _uses(await _logbook_for(hass_ws_client, hass, EXTERNAL_TARGET))
    assert len(uses) == 1
    assert uses[0]["entity_id"] == EXTERNAL_TARGET
    assert uses[0]["name"] == "test1"
    assert uses[0]["message"] == "used a PIN"

    # The source can hold the code that was typed; it is never where the
    # entry is filed.
    assert _uses(await _logbook_for(hass_ws_client, hass, EXTERNAL_KEYPAD)) == []


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    ("credential_type", "operation"),
    list(itertools.product(CredentialType, CredentialOperation)),
)
def test_every_use_reads_as_a_sentence_naming_its_kind(
    credential_type: CredentialType, operation: CredentialOperation
):
    """
    Every kind and operation has a message, and only a known operation is named.

    The logbook prints the user's name in front of the message, so it has to
    read on from a name. Exhaustive rather than sampled: the space is small
    and a new member of either enum must not ship without words.
    """
    message = credential_use_message(credential_type, operation)

    assert message.startswith("used ")
    assert str(credential_type) not in ("", message)
    if operation is CredentialOperation.UNKNOWN:
        assert " to " not in message
    else:
        assert message.endswith(f" to {operation}")

"""
A credential use is written to the logbook of what it was used against.

Home Assistant's logbook shows an entity only its own integration's described
events, and Lock Code Manager owns none of the locks it manages. So the entry
has to be a manual logbook entry, the one kind of event the logbook shows for
any entity whose ``entity_id`` it names. These tests query the logbook the way
a lock's more-info dialog does -- by the lock's entity ID -- so they fail if
the entry lands anywhere a person looking at the lock would not see it.
"""

from datetime import timedelta
import itertools
from typing import Any

import pytest
from pytest_homeassistant_custom_component.components.recorder.common import (
    async_wait_recording_done,
)

from homeassistant.components.logbook import DOMAIN as LOGBOOK_DOMAIN
from homeassistant.core import HomeAssistant
from homeassistant.setup import async_setup_component
from homeassistant.util import dt as dt_util

from custom_components.lock_code_manager.const import (
    ATTR_CODE,
    ATTR_SOURCE,
    ATTR_TARGET,
    DOMAIN,
    SERVICE_USE_CREDENTIAL,
)
from custom_components.lock_code_manager.model.credentials import CredentialType
from custom_components.lock_code_manager.model.events import (
    CredentialOperation,
    credential_use_message,
)
from custom_components.lock_code_manager.providers import BaseLock

from .common import LOCK_1_ENTITY_ID, LOCK_2_ENTITY_ID

EXTERNAL_KEYPAD = "sensor.side_gate_keypad"
EXTERNAL_TARGET = "cover.side_gate"


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def auto_enable_custom_integrations(recorder_db_url, enable_custom_integrations):
    """
    Claim the recorder database before Home Assistant starts.

    Overrides the project-wide autouse fixture of the same name, which pulls
    in `hass` before `recorder_db_url` may run.
    """
    yield


@pytest.fixture(name="logbook")
async def logbook_fixture(recorder_mock, hass: HomeAssistant) -> None:
    """Run the real logbook over the real recorder."""
    assert await async_setup_component(hass, LOGBOOK_DOMAIN, {})
    await hass.async_block_till_done()


async def _logbook_for(hass_ws_client, hass: HomeAssistant, entity_id: str) -> list:
    """Return the logbook entries for one entity, as its more-info dialog asks."""
    await async_wait_recording_done(hass)
    client = await hass_ws_client(hass)
    await client.send_json_auto_id(
        {
            "type": "logbook/get_events",
            "start_time": (dt_util.utcnow() - timedelta(hours=1)).isoformat(),
            "entity_ids": [entity_id],
        }
    )
    response = await client.receive_json()
    assert response["success"], response
    return response["result"]


def _uses(entries: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    """Keep the entries Lock Code Manager wrote, dropping the lock's own states."""
    return [entry for entry in entries if entry.get("domain") == DOMAIN]


async def test_a_lock_observed_use_is_in_the_locks_logbook(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    hass_ws_client,
    logbook,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
):
    """One use the lock observed is one entry on that lock, naming the user."""
    lock: BaseLock = lock_code_manager_config_entry.runtime_data.locks[LOCK_1_ENTITY_ID]
    lock.async_fire_code_slot_event(2, False, credential_type=CredentialType.PIN)
    await hass.async_block_till_done()

    uses = _uses(await _logbook_for(hass_ws_client, hass, LOCK_1_ENTITY_ID))
    assert len(uses) == 1
    assert uses[0]["entity_id"] == LOCK_1_ENTITY_ID
    assert uses[0]["name"] == "test2"
    assert uses[0]["message"] == "used a PIN to unlock"

    assert _uses(await _logbook_for(hass_ws_client, hass, LOCK_2_ENTITY_ID)) == []


async def test_a_reported_use_is_in_its_targets_logbook(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    hass_ws_client,
    logbook,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
):
    """
    A use reported through the action lands on its target, whatever that is.

    The target here is a cover no integration even provides: the entry names
    it, so the logbook files it there.
    """
    await hass.services.async_call(
        DOMAIN,
        SERVICE_USE_CREDENTIAL,
        {
            "config_entry_id": lock_code_manager_config_entry.entry_id,
            ATTR_CODE: "1234",
            ATTR_SOURCE: EXTERNAL_KEYPAD,
            ATTR_TARGET: EXTERNAL_TARGET,
        },
        blocking=True,
    )
    await hass.async_block_till_done()

    uses = _uses(await _logbook_for(hass_ws_client, hass, EXTERNAL_TARGET))
    assert len(uses) == 1
    assert uses[0]["entity_id"] == EXTERNAL_TARGET
    assert uses[0]["name"] == "test1"
    assert uses[0]["message"] == "used a PIN"

    # The source can hold the code that was typed; it is never where the
    # entry is filed.
    assert _uses(await _logbook_for(hass_ws_client, hass, EXTERNAL_KEYPAD)) == []


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    ("credential_type", "operation"),
    list(itertools.product(CredentialType, CredentialOperation)),
)
def test_every_use_reads_as_a_sentence_naming_its_kind(
    credential_type: CredentialType, operation: CredentialOperation
):
    """
    Every kind and operation has a message, and only a known operation is named.

    The logbook prints the user's name in front of the message, so it has to
    read on from a name. Exhaustive rather than sampled: the space is small
    and a new member of either enum must not ship without words.
    """
    message = credential_use_message(credential_type, operation)

    assert message.startswith("used ")
    if operation is CredentialOperation.UNKNOWN:
        assert " to " not in message
    else:
        assert message.endswith(f" to {operation}")


@pytest.mark.parametrize("operation", list(CredentialOperation))
def test_no_two_kinds_read_the_same(operation: CredentialOperation):
    """A card read and a fingerprint must not both read as the same use."""
    messages = {credential_use_message(kind, operation) for kind in CredentialType}
    assert len(messages) == len(CredentialType)

content.thinking:
I'm sketching out a CredentialUse type with fields for timestamp, target, and operation details, then planning a new credential-uses module with a usage limit of 10 within a 30-day window, plus a function to build the WebSocket query for fetching credential uses by entity.

For parsing, I'm filtering compressed history entries by valid dates, deduping, sorting, and mapping friendly names from the entity states. I want each use described like "Front Door — PIN, unlocked — 5 min ago," with kind labels (PIN, RFID tag, Fingerprint, Face, Password, NFC tag) and operation labels (Unlocked, Locked).

On the card itself, I'm adding expansion state for the uses list, toggling a chevron icon between right and down, refetching data each time it's expanded, and rendering rows with relative timestamps plus a "Full history" link that opens the more-info event history view.

For loading/error/empty states I'll show "Loading…", "Couldn't load history", and "No uses in the recorder's history" respectively, and I should also refetch while expanded if last_used changes so new uses appear live. I'm being careful never to read the source sensor's state since it could contain a cleartext code — only the target entity matters. I also want to verify the history_during_period websocket command's parameters and response shape against the HA core source to make sure I'm using it correctly.

content.text:
I hadn't written it yet; here it is. It assumes A and C ship in the next release, which isn't out yet, so it gives the workaround for now and avoids promising a version number.

---

> You're not missing anything. Lock Code Manager records the information, but Home Assistant doesn't show it in either place you looked.
>
> **Why the lock says "No cause was recorded":** that field only gets filled when something inside Home Assistant caused the change, like an automation or a button you pressed in the UI. A keypad or fingerprint unlock happens on the lock itself. The lock integration reports the new state, and Lock Code Manager hears separately which user it was. Lock Code Manager can't attach that to the lock's state change, so that line will keep saying it.
>
> **What's coming in the next release:**
> - **Each use goes into the logbook of the lock it was used on.** Open Front Door Lock's activity (or the Logbook page, filtered to that lock) and you'll see "Alice used a PIN to unlock" right next to the "Unlocked" entry. Card readers, fingerprint and face recognition show up the same way on locks that report which kind was used.
> - **Clicking "Last used" on the user card lists their recent uses.** Each one shows which lock, what kind of credential and whether it locked or unlocked, plus when. A "Full history" link underneath opens the complete history.
>
> **Until then:** you can get the logbook entries now with the [Credential Used blueprint](https://my.home-assistant.io/redirect/blueprint_import/?blueprint_url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Framan325%2Flock_code_manager%2Fblob%2Fmain%2Fblueprints%2Fautomation%2Flock_code_manager%2Fcredential_used.yaml). Leave its filters empty and use this as the action:
>
> ```yaml
> - action: logbook.log
>   data:
>     name: "{{ name }}"
>     message: "used a {{ credential_type }} to {{ operation }}"
>     entity_id: "{{ target }}"
> ```
>
> Once you've updated, delete that automation, or you'll see every use twice.
>
> Some limits that will still apply:
> - Only uses the lock tied to a user show up. The thumb-turn and remote commands that don't name a user won't appear.
> - Fingerprint and face only show up separately from PIN on locks that report which kind was used. Today that's Matter (fingerprint and face) and some Zigbee2MQTT locks (fingerprint).
> - The card's list only goes back as far as Home Assistant keeps history, which is 10 days by default. The logbook entries are kept for the same period.

---

Where the code is: A is done, and its end-to-end tests pass against the real logbook and recorder. They query the lock's logbook the same way its activity view does. C is wired into the card, and the TypeScript suite passes with the four old click-opens-more-info tests rewritten. I'm in the middle of adding a test that clicks the row and checks the rendered list. After that come the full Python run (still going in the background), `prek`, `yarn build`, a code review, and the PR. Nothing is committed yet.

All hooks are now passing after the initial failure flagged the rebuilt bundle. Before committing, I'll run a code review on the diff since previous reviews have consistently caught real issues.

Going through the memories to triage which issues are real. The commit race condition looks genuine - instead of refetching data on a new use event, I realize the entity's current state attributes already contain the target, credential_type, and operation info, so I can merge that directly into the parsed list without a refetch.

For the previous-owner-same-entity-id concern, I'm weighing whether this is actually a bug or just standard HA behavior - when a user is removed and a new one reuses the same slot, the entity ID carries forward and the recorder's history naturally retains old states under that ID. This matches how HA's more-info history graph works for any entity, so I'm inclined to treat this as expected platform behavior rather than something to fix.

Context enrichment on credential use events would be a nice enhancement but feels like scope creep, so I'll just note it. Similarly, the logbook showing a dropped credential kind isn't really wrong since the underlying bus event did fire - worth mentioning but not fixing.

The trickier issue is pre-6.0 rows: before the unified payload, the event_type field held the lock entity ID itself with no target, so anyone who upgraded within the last 30 days would have legacy rows mixed in. The cleanest fix is to simply skip rows that lack a proper string target rather than trying to reconstruct meaning from the old format - losing a few old entries is an acceptable tradeoff for correctness.

The flicker issue should already be resolved by avoiding refetches on new credential use. For labeling, I want to check whether the component's strings.json has translations for event_type values that I could use via formatEntityAttributeValue, since that would keep things consistent with how HA normally localizes these strings rather than hardcoding English everywhere. Fetch cost is also already addressed by only fetching on expand, so I can leave that alone. On the architecture side, firing EVENT_LOGBOOK_ENTRY manually via the public API was a deliberate choice over importing logbook directly into the model layer, though I should double check the real cost of that import since logbook pulls in recorder.

I see the real defect now: without refetching, the intermediate SECOND entry disappears from the open list once the state moves to THIRD, since it only existed in the current snapshot, not the history. I need to accumulate past states rather than relying solely on the current reference.

To fix this, I'll track observed rows while expanded by appending the current event state to a persisted _useRows array whenever it changes, deduping by state. I'll hook this both into the hass setter (so it catches state changes in production) and into the subscription data handler (so it also works in tests where hass isn't re-set), while still keeping the render-time merge to cover the gap before the first hass update.

I've confirmed this is a genuine bug: use 2 only existed as the current state and got overwritten when use 3 came along, dropping it from the open list. I'll fix this by having the card retain every current state it's seen while the list remains open.

input.command:
cat > /tmp/pr-body.md <<'EOF'
## Proposed change

A forum user asked how to see who unlocked which door, and when. The data was already recorded: the user's `credential_used` event entity holds `target`, `credential_type` and `operation` for every use. But Home Assistant didn't show it anywhere they'd look. The lock's activity said "No cause was recorded", and clicking **Last used** on the user card opened a more-info dialog that showed only the event type ("pin").

**1. Each use goes into the logbook of what it was used against.** `async_fire_credential_used` (the one function every use goes through, whether a lock reported it or `use_credential` was called) now also calls `logbook.async_log_entry(name, message, domain=lock_code_manager, entity_id=target)`. The lock's activity, the lock's device page and the Logbook filtered to that lock all show entries like "Alice used a PIN to unlock".

Why a manual entry instead of a `logbook.py` that describes our own event:
- When the logbook builds an entity's view, it only includes custom events from the integrations that own that entity (`async_determine_event_types`). For a lock, that's Z-Wave JS or Matter, never us.
- The query also matches on an `entity_id` or `device_id` key in the event data, and our payload has `target`.
- So a described event would only reach the unfiltered Logbook. A manual `logbook_entry` is the one event type the logbook includes for any entity named in its `entity_id`.

Precedent, for the record:
- No core integration writes `logbook_entry`.
- Of the 92 most-installed custom integrations I could check, one does: Better Thermostat, and only on its own entity.
- Integrations that act on another integration's entity (Alexa, HomeKit) get credit by calling the service with a shared context ID. That doesn't work here, because LCM doesn't make the lock's state change; it only hears about it afterwards.
- So this uses a public API somewhere no integration has needed to before. If lock integrations ever gain a way to record who unlocked, that should replace this.

This doesn't fill in "No cause was recorded" on the lock's own state row. The frontend builds the cause from shared context IDs, and the lock integration sets that context. The use shows up as its own row next to the state change.

**2. The user card lists recent uses.** Clicking **Last used** now expands the user's recent uses, up to 10. Each row shows what the credential was used against, the kind of credential, what the device did, and when. **Full history** underneath opens the more-info dialog, which is what clicking the row used to do.
- The list comes from the recorder's history of the event entity (`history/history_during_period`, last 30 days, attributes included). Nothing new is stored.
- Uses that happen while the list is open are added from the entity's current state. History isn't read again, because the recorder commits in batches and wouldn't have the new use yet.
- Rows recorded before 6.0, which have no `target`, are skipped.
- The `source` entity is never read, since its state can be the code that was typed.
- The labels for each kind match the event type translations in `strings.json`, and a contract test keeps them in sync.

**Messages are English, not translated.** LCM ships only `en.json`, and the cards are hard-coded English, so translating at write time would serve no one.

### Review findings not addressed here

I ran `/code-review` and fixed the commit race, the flicker on reload, rows from before 6.0, the label mismatch and the enum comparison. Left as they are:
- **History of a reused entity ID shows up under the new user.** If a removed user's name is reused, the new user's list includes the old user's uses. Home Assistant's own history does the same when an entity ID is reused.
- **The logbook entry carries no context.** So a `use_credential` call from an automation doesn't show "triggered by automation". That's worth a separate follow-up.
- **The logbook also records uses the event entity drops** because their kind isn't in its event types. This matches the bus event, which fires for them too.
- **`model/events.py` imports `homeassistant.components.logbook`.** That's deliberate: it's the public API, and the logbook is part of `default_config`.

### Testing

- `tests/test_logbook.py`: end-to-end with the real recorder and logbook, querying `logbook/get_events` by the lock's entity ID, the same way its activity view does. Covers a use the lock reported, a use reported through `use_credential` against a cover, and that nothing is filed under the source. Also checks every pairing of kind and operation, and that no two kinds read the same. Mutation check: filing under `source` instead of `target` fails.
- `ts/credential-uses.test.ts`: the history parser.
- `ts/slot-card.dom.test.ts`: clicks the rendered row and reads the list, including a use that arrives while the list is open and a failed history read. Mutation checks: removing the expand, or removing the step that keeps the current state, fails.
- `tests/test_frontend_contract.py`: the card's labels match `strings.json`.
- Full Python suite run serially: everything passes. Under `-n auto`, three real-time pacing tests fail from load and pass on their own; they don't involve credential uses.
- `yarn build` prints an existing type error in `ts/generate-view.ts` (`pinActiveEntity`), a file this PR doesn't touch.

## Type of change

- [ ] Dependency upgrade
- [ ] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [x] New feature (which adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix/feature causing existing functionality to break)
- [ ] Code quality improvements to existing code or addition of tests

## Additional information

- This PR fixes or closes issue: none filed; it came from a forum question
- This PR is related to issue:

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

This doesn't fill in "No cause was recorded" on the lock's own state row. The frontend builds the cause from shared context IDs, and the lock integration sets that context. The use shows up as its own row next to the state change.

**2. The user card lists recent uses.** Clicking **Last used** now expands the user's recent uses, up to 10. Each row shows what the credential was used against, the kind of credential, what the device did, and when. **Full history** underneath opens the more-info dialog, which is what clicking the row used to do.
- The list comes from the recorder's history of the event entity (`history/history_during_period`, last 30 days, attributes included). Nothing new is stored.
- Uses that happen while the list is open are added from the entity's current state. History isn't read again, because the recorder commits in batches and wouldn't have the new use yet.
- Rows recorded before 6.0, which have no `target`, are skipped.
- The `source` entity is never read, since its state can be the code that was typed.
- The labels for each kind match the event type translations in `strings.json`, and a contract test keeps them in sync.

**Messages are English, not translated.** LCM ships only `en.json`, and the cards are hard-coded English, so translating at write time would serve no one.

### Review findings not addressed here

I ran `/code-review` and fixed the commit race, the flicker on reload, rows from before 6.0, the label mismatch and the enum comparison. Left as they are:
- **History of a reused entity ID shows up under the new user.** If a removed user's name is reused, the new user's list includes the old user's uses. Home Assistant's own history does the same when an entity ID is reused.
- **The logbook entry carries no context.** So a `use_credential` call from an automation doesn't show "triggered by automation". That's worth a separate follow-up.
- **The logbook also records uses the event entity drops** because their kind isn't in its event types. This matches the bus event, which fires for them too.
- **`model/events.py` imports `homeassistant.components.logbook`.** That's deliberate: it's the public API, and the logbook is part of `default_config`.

### Testing

- `tests/test_logbook.py`: end-to-end with the real recorder and logbook, querying `logbook/get_events` by the lock's entity ID, the same way its activity view does. Covers a use the lock reported, a use reported through `use_credential` against a cover, and that nothing is filed under the source. Also checks every pairing of kind and operation, and that no two kinds read the same. Mutation check: filing under `source` instead of `target` fails.
- `ts/credential-uses.test.ts`: the history parser.
- `ts/slot-card.dom.test.ts`: clicks the rendered row and reads the list, including a use that arrives while the list is open and a failed history read. Mutation checks: removing the expand, or removing the step that keeps the current state, fails.
- `tests/test_frontend_contract.py`: the card's labels match `strings.json`.
- Full Python suite run serially: everything passes. Under `-n auto`, three real-time pacing tests fail from load and pass on their own; they don't involve credential uses.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

content.text:
I've opened [PR #1796](https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1796) with A and C, built in the worktree `.worktrees/credential-use-logbook`.

**What it does**
- **A, the logbook:** every credential use is now written to the logbook of whatever it was used against, as "Alice used a PIN to unlock". It shows up in the lock's activity, on its device page, and in the Logbook filtered to that lock. This works for uses a lock reports and for uses reported through `use_credential`. Tests run the real logbook and recorder and ask for the lock's entries the same way its activity view does.
- **C, the card:** clicking **Last used** now opens a list of the user's last 10 uses, each showing the lock, the kind of credential, what the lock did, and when. A **Full history** link underneath opens the more-info dialog, which is what the click used to do. The list is read from the history Home Assistant already keeps, so nothing new is stored.

**Where I changed the plan**
- **No translated messages.** LCM ships only `en.json` and the cards are hard-coded English, so translating the logbook text would have served no one. I kept it English and said so in the PR.
- **Two real bugs from the code review, now fixed.**
  - Re-reading history right after a use missed that use, because the recorder saves in batches.
  - My first fix for that dropped a use from the open list when the next one arrived.
  
  The card now adds new uses from the entity's current state instead of re-reading history, and a test clicks through that case.
- **Card labels now match `strings.json`** ("RFID" rather than "RFID tag"), with a test keeping the two in sync.
- **Four review findings I didn't fix,** each explained in the PR:
  - a new user who reuses a removed user's name sees the old user's uses (Home Assistant's own history does the same);
  - a use reported by an automation isn't linked to that automation in the logbook (a follow-up);
  - the logbook also records uses the event entity ignores;
  - the event code imports the logbook component directly.

**Tests:** everything passes: the full Python suite run serially, `yarn test` (731 tests) and `prek`. Each new test was also checked against a deliberately broken version of the code, and it failed as it should. Two things to know:
- Under `-n auto`, three timing-sensitive pacing tests fail. They pass on their own and on main, and don't involve credential uses.
- `yarn build` prints a type error in `ts/generate-view.ts`, a file this PR doesn't touch.

**Forum reply:** the draft from earlier still matches what was built, so you can post it once this is released. One small mismatch: the card will say "RFID", not "card reader".

Copilot's review comments haven't come in yet. When they do, I'll go through them, and per AGENTS.md I'll check with you before committing any changes.
